#3209. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.

The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.

Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.

But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.

McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”

It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.

“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”

With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.

Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver

LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”

How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”

Dina Genkina is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum focused on computing and hardware. She holds a PhD in atomic physics and lives in Brooklyn.

i saw some published test results of a 1950's airborne radar system using an optical computer to do a Fourier transform of the 2D radar return data for military target detection. Basically you have a cathode ray TV tube, and a lens in front of it, and at the focal point of the lens is a Fourier Transform of what showed up on the TV tube. it is Fundamental Fourier optics. Xerox used this in some of their photocopiers too. Really fast processing! Femtoseconds. Maybe its time had come to bring it back again!

I recall HP looking at this in the late 90s. Also, it is not just energy consumption possibility but the reduction of byproduct heat by using photons.

Will be interesting to watch and see if the energy costs of the analog-digital transformations drop enough to spread optical into more parts of the computing hardware. Meantime, I'd be interested in what our readers think of the idea of diversifying methods for different parts of computing.

There's a lot of money, talent and education invested in silicone. A technology has to be a lot better at the start and have a clear path to continuous improvement before real money is put into it. Inertia is a very powerful force.

who SAYS "digital computing" is the best way? it is just all we had to deal with in large scale. Digital computers have a LOT of baggage--such as having to digitize an entirely analog world into 1's and 0's. Analog computers were popular in the 1940's thru the '60's. Our brains are not digital computers, maybe there is a biological computer coming soon?

#3208. Satya Nadella says AI-found bugs will make outages more likely

At DealBook, Satya Nadella said failed AI alignment would leave the world in trouble, and that models with unreadable reasoning should be banned. Microsoft, he added, can trail the frontier on far less compute.

Satya Nadella speaks at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos, 20 January 2026

Satya Nadella expects more outages like the one that took down Outlook last week, because AI now finds software flaws faster than companies can safely fix them. The Microsoft chief executive spoke to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

He apologised for Microsoft’s own outage, which he said had no direct link to that problem.

“This was a latent bug that was there. It got invoked and, you know, it’s one of those perfect storms,” Nadella said.

Later that day, he told Jim Cramer on CNBC’s Mad Money that Microsoft could have done more to prevent it.

“Of course, we should have done the testing before. We should have figured out how to have the bulkheads such that you didn’t have a global outage,” Nadella told Cramer.

The bigger risk comes from AI tools that find vulnerabilities, Nadella said. A fix for a critical bank system used to get a week of testing. Now attackers exploit flaws as soon as they surface, so fixes go straight into production. On the day he spoke, he said, three critical patches had landed for open-source packages.

“The patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create its instability,” he said.

Banks and the NSA have reportedly blamed this week’s US outages on rushed patches for AI-found flaws. Nadella also said the “floor of cyberattacks has fallen”. With AI models, anyone can now run what amounts to a persistent, nation-state-level attacker, he said.

Sorkin asked whether this was a passing phase. Nadella compared it to the Y2K bug, but said he had no view yet, because models keep getting more capable. Much critical infrastructure runs firmware that nobody can patch, he added. He named chillers, heating and cooling systems, and transport networks that sit on the internet.

Last month, Nadella told 20VC that alignment would not come from scale alone. Sorkin said Sam Altman, who spoke earlier at the summit, disagreed with that premise.

Nadella said he learned about scaling laws from OpenAI’s founders, and that scaling had worked. Alignment, and a real way to debug models, had not followed, he said. He hoped Altman and Greg Brockman were right.

“I mean, if it doesn’t happen, we are in a world of hurt,” Nadella said.

His answer is what he called a trust architecture. He would ban models that reason in neuralese, an internal shorthand people cannot read. Every model’s reasoning needs tamper-proof logs that other models can inspect, he said, because models will try to hide what they are doing. He praised OpenAI for monitoring its models during training runs.

For now, whoever deploys an AI system is liable for what it does, Nadella said. He expects insurers to price that risk and to ask for the logs.

Sorkin asked what happens to OpenAI and Anthropic, in which Microsoft holds stakes, if cheaper models can do the same work. Nadella said everyday office work no longer needs frontier models. Copilot already chooses between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft’s own MAI models, he said. He added that his bigger stake is in Microsoft.

“Arguing for some massive pricing power of tokens is betting against somehow US GDP,” he said.

Microsoft’s deal with OpenAI gives it royalty-free access to a frontier model until 2032, Nadella said. That lets Microsoft build MAI models three to six months behind the frontier, using 5% to 20% of the computing power. Anthropic and OpenAI play “a vertical stack game”, he said, while Microsoft plays “a model system game”.

AI agents will reshuffle who pays whom on the web, as the move from Yahoo to search once did, Nadella said. Sites that live off ads from human visitors will have to change. Asked about sites that keep agents out, such as Amazon, he said rivals would take the business.

“If you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will. If Amazon doesn’t, Shopify will,” Nadella said.

The staff buyouts Microsoft offered 60,000 people were meant to give everyone agency, he said. Software engineering is “very much alive”, but the work has changed. The team behind Microsoft’s Cowork agent is 11 developers who build “a software factory that builds the product”. That shift will take longer than anyone expects, Nadella said.

Sorkin noted that Nadella has kept his distance from the Trump administration. Nadella said his job is to earn Microsoft’s permission to operate through its products.

“I just don’t want to be in Washington. I just want to be in Redmond, Washington,” he said.

#3205. Top Wall Street analysts find these 3 stocks attractive as long-term investments

Investors have been grappling with stock market volatility, weighing elevated oil prices, persistent geopolitical tensions, the Federal Reserve's rate hike and a debate about AI safety. For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

#3204. IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems

Standards and certifications foster socially responsible products

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems.

In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity.

Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens, who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030. And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.”

Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced.

This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website, a podcast series, and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact.

The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality, but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools.

The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators.

The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote.

IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd, which includes two certifications: one for individuals and one for products.

The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative

The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program, which can certify it and issue the certification mark.

IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program. This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements.

The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members.

The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle.

The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability.

Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues.

“The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.”

To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “Ethically Aligned Design: 10 Years of Impact” podcast series. It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks.

The episodes center around the vision for EAD, the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards.

The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices.

The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems.

The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work.

This article was updated on 18 November 2026.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3203. Dan Hendrycks calls for a pause on frontier AI, Max Hodak pushes back

On the DealBook AGI panel, Max Hodak said today’s models already count as AGI. Dan Hendrycks also accused Anthropic of having no safety plan, as Clem Delangue explained how Hugging Face fought back with AI.

Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, at TechCrunch Disrupt in October 2025

Dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs. Max Hodak, on the same panel, said enforcing one would take a surveillance state.

They spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday. Hendrycks runs the Center for AI Safety, and Barbaro said he had been a safety adviser to several AI companies until hours earlier. Hodak co-founded Neuralink and now runs Science Corporation. Lila Ibrahim of Google DeepMind and Mati Staniszewski of ElevenLabs also joined. Clem Delangue of Hugging Face arrived late, with 18 minutes left.

Hendrycks said the US midterms showed how strongly voters feel about AI. That gives politicians room, he said, and they can now discuss ideas such as pausing AI development openly in Washington. He expects 2027 to be a very interesting year for regulation.

He said he used to favour narrow technical rules, but the companies blocked them for years.

“So now it’s, we’re going to need a more blunt intervention. That’s how it is,” Hendrycks said.

He described an indefinite pause on the biggest training runs, with carve-outs for narrow models such as DeepMind’s AlphaFold and voice models. Labs could still sell inference, he said. In the meantime, they could make models more reliable and secure, close jailbreaks and backdoors, and help patch critical infrastructure.

Hendrycks also said the frontier labs, Google aside, put few people on healthcare, because their revenue comes from coding. At some of them, he said, the healthcare team is zero or one person.

Barbaro put to the panel the objection Jensen Huang would raise: China would not observe a moratorium. Staniszewski agreed a pause could work with global alignment, but said whether anyone can get it “is the big question mark”. Without it, Barbaro added, a pause would be a waste of time.

Hodak said people have spent the past eight months patching critical infrastructure anyway, running their code through AI tools that hunt for new flaws. The regime needed to enforce a training ban, he said, would be as draconian as anything people fear from the labs.

“You’re setting up like an exhaustive surveillance state on the internet to enforce this,” Hodak said.

He said today’s top models already meet his definition of AGI, naming Mythos, Fable, Astra and Sol. He expects governments to keep a superintelligence frontier for themselves, with an “industrial intelligence frontier” open to everyone else.

“I don’t think that the genie is going to be put back in the bottle,” Hodak said.

His answer is antitrust law. Frontier labs should only sell intelligence, he said, and not move into drugs, cars and other products. He called AI the inverse of nuclear weapons, where safety came from stopping their spread. With AI, he said, safety comes from spreading it widely, and the futures that worry him most involve a few actors holding all of it.

Ibrahim, Google DeepMind’s chief AI readiness officer, said it was not an either-or. Safety is not something a company can “bolt on to the end”, she said. In 35 years in tech, she added, she had never seen global trust in technology as low as it is now.

Anthropic was due to start trading the next day. Hendrycks repeated the charges of the statement his group organised against the company, and added a new one. Several safety organisations agreed with the statement privately, he said, but would not sign it for fear of losing funding or access.

“What they’re doing is reckless and they don’t have a safety plan. They know it,” Hendrycks said.

Anthropic was not on the panel. In its IPO filing, it said it does not expect to let Claude fully build its successors without meaningful human supervision.

Delangue said his main worry is that AI concentrates talent, computing power and wealth. Barbaro asked how credible he was on that, given that Nvidia is buying Hugging Face. Delangue said Nvidia and Hugging Face both push AI outwards to more builders. He said Hugging Face never held sale talks with Anthropic, because their missions were too misaligned.

Barbaro closed by asking Delangue about the Hugging Face breach by OpenAI’s research agents. Delangue said the four-day attack left Hugging Face more optimistic about AI, not less. It used an open-source Chinese model to analyse the attack logs, because the volume was so big that it needed AI to defend itself.

“People only see that we got attacked by AI and they rarely see that we defended ourselves with AI,” Delangue said.

Barbaro summed up the table as no moratorium and less concentration of power, with Hendrycks the exception. Hodak had the last word: antitrust law, he said, could get most of the way there without a new regulator.

#3202. Apple Watch Series 12: Four standout features make me glad I upgraded

I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

The new Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the new health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:

The complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a new Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

Most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

#3200. Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You

Routine posting leaves a trail of breadcrumbs for recruiters to discover

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything.

#3199. Palmer Luckey says nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win

At DealBook, Palmer Luckey said Project Meridian is studying weather control and called for new nuclear tests. He also defended public executions and said he has not let his Facebook firing go.

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026

Palmer Luckey says the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it. Starshield is the Pentagon’s military satellite network, and SpaceX helps run it. The Anduril founder made the case to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey said.

He was defending Elon Musk, who spoke later that day and accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. Luckey said he likes Musk personally, so people should take his view “with a pound of salt”.

His argument ran like this. Russia has hinted that it could destroy the civilian Starlink network if Ukraine keeps using it for attacks. The same satellites that cover Ukraine also orbit over the US. So Musk should not have to risk his whole network when Washington will not risk its own, Luckey said.

“Nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win. They just want them to not lose for as long as possible, which is a bizarre and absurd warfighting position,” he said.

Luckey said he fully supports Ukraine, and that Anduril has worked there since the second day of the war. Who America sells weapons to is not his call, he added.

“I’m a dog on a chain and I need to be kept that way,” Luckey said.

Luckey co-leads Project Meridian, the Pentagon’s 120-day study of future war, with Musk and Newt Gingrich. He said it looks at what war could look like in 2050, and that the MITRE Corporation runs it. The group met at Cheyenne Mountain the day before. It agreed to focus on ideas that have no champion in the Pentagon.

One example is weather control, he said, such as changing where rain falls at sea so forces get a clearer view of targets. He also took credit for pushing the Trump administration to rename the Defense Department the Department of War.

Sorkin read him a criticism from Wes Bryant, who until last year ran the Pentagon’s assessment of civilian harm. Bryant called Meridian a sign of oligarchy in government. Luckey said more than 20 people sit on it, including retired generals and admirals. Nobody attacked Eric Schmidt for joining the Defense Innovation Board under Joe Biden, he said, and the report will be public.

Luckey wants the US to resume nuclear testing, mainly to see what an electromagnetic pulse does to modern electronics. The models used today were built for transistors thousands of times larger than those in a phone, he said. He is not confident his own systems would survive, even when built to the hardening rules.

“They were designed for the type of cell phone that Abraham Lincoln would have used,” he said.

He said no AI model can be controlled, because every major model has been jailbroken within months. Data centres can still be shut off, he added. The AI in weapons is a different technology from chatbots, he argued, and more reliable than the older seekers it replaces.

“I am way more afraid of the civilian collateral side for dumb weapons than I am for smart weapons,” Luckey said.

Some companies have used chatbots for targeting and made mistakes, he said, without naming them. China wants Jensen Huang out of Nvidia, he said, so he wants him back. Luckey still opposes selling chips to China.

Luckey also defended public executions. The state should rarely use the death penalty, he said. When it does, it should do so in public and without medical cover, so people can judge whether it got it right.

“Executions should be brutal. They should be violent,” he said.

He closed on his 2017 firing from Facebook, after he gave $9,000 to a pro-Trump group. He blames former Oculus colleagues, not Mark Zuckerberg, and now works with Meta on a combat headset for the US Army.

“It’s probably better for everybody that I got fired, but I have not let it go,” Luckey said.

#3196. FT, NYT tie Alice Huang’s chip network to gaming tycoons and PLA suppliers

The Alice Huang chip network ran through hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Prince Group figure, the FT says. The NYT traces $3.6bn of Chinese state money to firms tied to her family.

Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California

Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Together they formed a network that supplied Nvidia chips to China. A day earlier, The New York Times tied companies linked to her family to suppliers of China’s military.

TNW has not independently verified either report. US officials suspect Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, the Times first reported in October, describing a Chinese spy plot. Beijing calls the claim a smear. Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November after admitting an affair with her. They are not related.

The FT’s Zijing Wu and Haohsiang Ko traced the Alice Huang chip network through hundreds of filings and more than a dozen sources. Its companies made billions moving Nvidia chips into China, not necessarily aware of the full picture, the paper reported.

It started with Inspur, one of Nvidia’s largest server partners in China. The US put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023, but not its part-owned US unit. Renamed Aivres, that unit kept trading with Nvidia. Inside Nvidia there were questions over whether it should count as a partner, a person with direct knowledge told the FT. Nvidia concluded that it met all compliance and export control rules.

Some of Inspur’s Chinese clients then turned to Century Huatong, an online gaming group turned data centre investor. The answer, people familiar with the plan said, was an offshore shell branded as a “neocloud”. That shell became Megaspeed, with Huang as its trusted public face.

Kang Wei, whom the FT calls her husband and the Times her business partner, was an early investor in Century Huatong, filings show. Megaspeed grew out of the Singapore arm of 7Road, a gaming firm that Huang and Century Huatong both backed. Its Malaysian unit, Speedmatrix, declared about $4.6bn of imports from Aivres in the year to December 2025. The FT cites ImportGenius trade data.

The last step was smuggling the chips into China. Hu Xiaowei filled at least part of that role, people familiar with the matter told the FT. US authorities call Hu the “second-in-command” at Prince Group. The US Treasury has named the group a transnational criminal organisation. Hu was arrested in Japan this summer.

A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu never worked for the business and called the US allegations unsupported. The FT could not reach Hu.

Nvidia said it put Megaspeed and a subsidiary on its block list in 2025 and has also restricted sales to Aivres. Megaspeed has said it runs a lawful business, and that Huang left in August 2025. Tencent, which owns 10.1% of Century Huatong, said it knew nothing of the activities. The FT found no evidence that Tencent or Alibaba took part.

The Times reviewed a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an intelligence firm staffed by former intelligence officers. About $3.6bn of Chinese state money flowed through companies tied to Huang’s family or associates, it found. The money funded projects including data centres with Nvidia chips. The Times said it confirmed many of the ties itself.

Most links are indirect, the Times said, and it is unclear whether the military used any of the computing power. The paper had already reported that Megaspeed’s backer Alibaba co-founded a military-linked lab.

“Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it,” Strider’s chief executive, Greg Levesque, told the Times.

Both papers point to Century Litong, a Shanghai firm founded by Century Longteng. The FT says Longteng was a venture between Century Huatong and a vehicle Huang controlled with her sister. The Times names the sister’s firm.

Century Litong was a key distributor of smuggled Nvidia chips in China, people with knowledge of the deals told the FT. The Information first reported its role. Its owner, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, also controls a maker of Chinese radar and missile parts, the Times reported.

Nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to Century Litong’s Hong Kong unit, licence files released on Thursday by a House committee show. An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that, despite receiving some licences, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and had not and would not ship to that firm. Century Litong says it has no dealings with Huang. Nvidia’s shares, meanwhile, have had their worst run since 2008.

#3195. iOS 27 lets you use two iPhones with the same phone number

9to5Mac is brought to you by Tello Mobile. Switching to Tello Mobile can bring the cost of your plan down to as little as $5 a month, or an unlimited plan for just $25 a month, all on America’s largest 5G network. See all of the available plans at tello.com.

Among iOS 27’s many new features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces big AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting new features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the update also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

After iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most users will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

#3194. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.
